paper.title: Expected PGT paper 2 · most-repeated ideas
paper.source: Written by GS HOUSE for the UP PGT Mathematics exam expected in December 2026, in the pattern of the UP PGT paper of 10 May 2026 and the official syllabus: 32 questions asked in earlier papers (24 from UP PGT 2021 and 8 from UP PGT 2011; each solved again, misprints repaired) and 58 new; every question checked by a second mathematician

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q1 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: The value of $5^2 + 6^2 + 7^2 + \dots + 20^2$ is:
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP

en.q: The number of elements of order 2 in the symmetric group $S_4$ is:
en.explanation: A permutation has order 2 exactly when it is a product of disjoint transpositions. In $S_4$: transpositions $(a\ b)$, ${}^4C_2 = 6$ of them; products of two disjoint transpositions $(a\ b)(c\ d)$, $\frac12\,{}^4C_2 = 3$ of them. Total $6 + 3 = 9$.
notes: Counts only the double transpositions $(a\ b)(c\ d)$.
This is the number of even permutations, $|A_4| = 12$.
path: 4.4 Permutations and the symmetric group Sn
facts: Order of a permutation = l.c.m. of its cycle lengths. $S_4$ has 1 identity, 6 transpositions, 3 double transpositions, 8 three-cycles and 6 four-cycles.

en.q: $\int_0^{\pi/2} \log(\tan x)\,dx$ is equal to:
en.explanation: With $x \to \frac\pi2 - x$, $I = \int_0^{\pi/2}\log\cot x\,dx = -I$. So $2I = 0$ and $I = 0$.
notes: A value of a different king-property integral; here the integrand is odd about $x = \frac\pi4$.
facts: $\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q4 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: The differential equation of $y = ae^{-bx}$ ($a$ and $b$ are parameters) is:
en.explanation: $y' = -abe^{-bx} = -by$ and $y'' = b^2y$. Then $yy'' = b^2y^2 = (-by)^2 = (y')^2$, i.e. $y\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$.
facts: Two arbitrary constants are eliminated by differentiating twice: the equation is of order 2.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q5 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If $\omega\ (\ne 1)$ is a cube root of unity and $(1 + \omega)^7 = A + B\omega$, then the value of $A^2 + B^2$ is:
en.explanation: $1 + \omega = -\omega^2$, so $(1 + \omega)^7 = -\omega^{14} = -\omega^2 = 1 + \omega$. Hence $A = B = 1$ and $A^2 + B^2 = 2$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$ and $\omega^3 = 1$: reduce powers modulo 3.

en.q: The eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are:
en.explanation: If $AX = \lambda X$ with $X \ne 0$, then $A^2X = \lambda^2X$. Since $A^2 = A$, $\lambda^2X = \lambda X$, so $\lambda^2 = \lambda$ and $\lambda = 0$ or 1.
notes: Only a nilpotent matrix has all eigenvalues 0.
These are the possible eigenvalues of an involutory matrix ($A^2 = I$).
This describes a real skew-symmetric matrix.
facts: $A^2 = A \Rightarrow \lambda \in \{0, 1\}$; $A^2 = I \Rightarrow \lambda = \pm 1$; $A^k = O \Rightarrow \lambda = 0$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q7 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: If $\tan\theta\cdot\tan2\theta = 1$, then $\theta =$
en.explanation: $\tan\theta\tan2\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \cos\theta\cos2\theta - \sin\theta\sin2\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos3\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = (2n + 1)\frac\pi6$. But $\tan\theta$ must be defined, so the values $\theta = \frac\pi2 + k\pi$ (in this family when $2n + 1$ is a multiple of 3) must be removed. What remains is $\frac\pi6, \frac{5\pi}{6}, \frac{7\pi}{6}, \frac{11\pi}{6}, \dots = n\pi \pm \frac\pi6$.
facts: After reducing a tangent equation to sines and cosines, remove the values where the original tangents are undefined.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q8 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: The number of common tangents to the circles $x^2 + y^2 - x = 0$ and $x^2 + y^2 + x = 0$ is:
en.explanation: Centres $\left(\frac12, 0\right)$, $\left(-\frac12, 0\right)$, radii $\frac12, \frac12$. Distance between centres $= 1 = r_1 + r_2$: the circles touch externally (at the origin), so there are 3 common tangents.
notes: Four would mean the circles are separate.
Two would mean the circles intersect.
path: 11.8 Polar equation of a conic; common tangents (PGT)

en.q: If $y = x^2e^x$, then the value of $\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}$ at $x = 0$ is:
en.explanation: By Leibnitz's theorem, only three terms survive: $\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2e^x) = e^x\left[x^2 + 2nx + n(n - 1)\right]$. At $x = 0$ this is $n(n - 1)$.
notes: Keeps the middle term $2nx\,e^x$ but sets $x = 1$ there.
facts: Leibnitz: $(uv)_n = \sum_{k} {}^nC_k\, u_k\, v_{n-k}$; with $u = x^2$ only $k = 0, 1, 2$ survive.

en.q: The derivative of $\sin^{-1}x$ with respect to $\cos^{-1}x$ $(-1 < x < 1)$ is:
en.explanation: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$ and $\frac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$, so the required derivative is their quotient, $-1$. (Or: $\sin^{-1}x = \frac\pi2 - \cos^{-1}x$.)
notes: Sign error: the derivative of $\cos^{-1}x$ is negative.
This is the derivative of $\sin^{-1}x$ with respect to $x$.
facts: Derivative of $u$ with respect to $v$: $\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{du/dx}{dv/dx}$; and $\sin^{-1}x + \cos^{-1}x = \frac\pi2$.

en.q: A particle moves along a straight line so that the time $t$ and the distance $x$ are related by $t = ax^2 + bx$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $v$ is its velocity, its retardation is:
en.explanation: $\frac{dt}{dx} = 2ax + b$, so $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{1}{2ax + b}$. Acceleration $= v\frac{dv}{dx} = v \cdot \frac{-2a}{(2ax + b)^2} = -2a\,v \cdot v^2 = -2av^3$. So the retardation is $2av^3$.
notes: Uses $\frac{dv}{dx}$ for the acceleration instead of $v\frac{dv}{dx}$.
path: 15.8 Rectilinear motion and simple harmonic motion
facts: In a straight line: acceleration $= \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$; if $t$ is given in terms of $x$, then $v = 1\big/\frac{dt}{dx}$.

en.q: If $A$ is a nilpotent matrix of index 2, then for every positive integer $n$, $A(I + A)^n$ equals:
en.explanation: $I$ and $A$ commute, so $(I + A)^n = I + nA + {}^nC_2A^2 + \dots = I + nA$ because $A^2 = O$. Hence $A(I + A)^n = A + nA^2 = A$.
notes: Treats $A$ times anything as $O$; only $A^2 = O$.
This is $(I + A)^n$ itself, before multiplying by $A$.
facts: If $A^2 = O$, then $(I + A)^n = I + nA$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q13 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: If ${}^nP_r = 720 \cdot {}^nC_r$, then the value of $r$ is:
facts: ${}^nP_r = r!\,{}^nC_r$: choosing $r$ objects and then arranging them.

en.q: $\int \frac{dx}{1 + e^x}$ is equal to (where $C$ is an arbitrary constant):
en.explanation: $\frac{1}{1 + e^x} = 1 - \frac{e^x}{1 + e^x}$, so the integral is $x - \log(1 + e^x) + C$ (equivalently $-\log(1 + e^{-x}) + C$).
notes: Sign error: $-\log(1 + e^{-x})$ would be correct.
Its derivative is $\frac{e^x}{1 + e^x}$, the complement of the integrand.
Sign error: its derivative is $\frac{1 + 2e^x}{1 + e^x}$.
facts: Add and subtract $e^x$ in the numerator, or divide by $e^x$: $\int\frac{e^{-x}}{e^{-x} + 1}dx$.

en.q: Four letters are put at random into four addressed envelopes, one letter in each. The number of ways in which no letter goes into its correct envelope is:
en.explanation: This is the number of derangements of 4 objects: $D_4 = 4!\left(1 - \frac1{1!} + \frac1{2!} - \frac1{3!} + \frac1{4!}\right) = 24 - 24 + 12 - 4 + 1 = 9$.
notes: $4! - 1$: excludes only the arrangement with every letter correct.
$3!$: fixes one letter's envelope and arranges the rest, which is not the condition.
$4! - 9$: this counts the ways with at least one letter correct.

en.q: A die is thrown once. Given that the number shown is even, the probability that it is greater than 3 is:
en.explanation: Let $A$ = greater than 3 $= \{4, 5, 6\}$ and $B$ = even $= \{2, 4, 6\}$. $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{2/6}{3/6} = \frac23$.
notes: This is $P(A \cap B) = \frac26$, not divided by $P(B)$.
path: 16.2 Conditional probability, multiplication theorem, independent events
facts: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$: the condition shrinks the sample space to $B$.

en.q: Match List – I (Integral) with List – II (Value). List – I: a. $\int \tan x\,dx$, b. $\int \cot x\,dx$, c. $\int \sec x\,dx$, d. $\int \operatorname{cosec}x\,dx$. List – II: I. $\log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$, II. $\log|\sin x| + C$, III. $-\log|\cos x| + C$, IV. $\log|\operatorname{cosec}x - \cot x| + C$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: a – III, b – II, c – IV, d – I
a – IV, b – III, c – II, d – I
a – III, b – II, c – I, d – IV
a – II, b – III, c – I, d – IV
en.explanation: $\int\tan x\,dx = -\log|\cos x|$ (III); $\int\cot x\,dx = \log|\sin x|$ (II); $\int\sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x|$ (I); $\int\operatorname{cosec}x\,dx = \log|\operatorname{cosec}x - \cot x|$ (IV).
notes: Reads the lists in reverse order.
facts: $\int \sec x\,dx = \log|\sec x + \tan x|$ and $\int \operatorname{cosec}x\,dx = \log\left|\tan\frac x2\right|$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q18 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: The focus of the parabola $y^2 - 4y - 8x + 4 = 0$ is:
notes: Interchanges the coordinates of the focus.
Takes $a = 1$ and also misplaces the vertex.
facts: For $(y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h)$: vertex $(h, k)$, focus $(h + a, k)$, directrix $x = h - a$.

en.q: $\int x\sec^2 x\,dx$ is equal to (where $C$ is an arbitrary constant):
en.explanation: By parts with $u = x$, $dv = \sec^2x\,dx$: $\int x\sec^2x\,dx = x\tan x - \int\tan x\,dx = x\tan x + \log|\cos x| + C$.
notes: Sign error: $\int\tan x\,dx = -\log|\cos x|$ and it is subtracted.
Integrates both factors separately; not how a product is integrated.
facts: By parts: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$; take the algebraic factor as $u$.

en.q: If the roots of the equation $x^2 - bx + c = 0$ are two consecutive integers, then $b^2 - 4c$ equals:
en.explanation: If the roots are $n$ and $n + 1$, then $b^2 - 4c = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = (\alpha - \beta)^2 = 1$.
notes: Takes the difference of the roots as $\sqrt2$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: The discriminant of a monic quadratic is the square of the difference of its roots.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q21 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If $y = 4x - 5$ is the equation of the tangent to the curve $y^2 = ax^3 + b$ at $(2, 3)$, then $(a, b)$ is equal to:
en.explanation: $2yy' = 3ax^2$, so at $(2, 3)$: $y' = \frac{12a}{6} = 2a$. The tangent has slope 4, so $a = 2$. The point lies on the curve: $9 = 2 \cdot 8 + b$, so $b = -7$.
facts: A tangent at a point gives two conditions: equal slopes and the point on the curve.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q22 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: The area of the region bounded by the curve $y = x^3$, the $x$-axis and the ordinates $x = -2$ and $x = 1$ is:
en.explanation: The curve is below the axis on $[-2, 0]$. Area $= \left|\int_{-2}^0x^3dx\right| + \int_0^1x^3dx = \left|-4\right| + \frac14 = \frac{17}{4}$. (The signed integral $-\frac{15}{4}$ is not the area.)
facts: Area = integral of $|y|$; split where the curve crosses the axis.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q23 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If the difference of the roots of the equation $x^2 + px + 12 = 0$ is one, then the values of $p$ are:
en.explanation: $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = p^2 - 48 = 1$, so $p^2 = 49$ and $p = \pm 7$ (roots $-3, -4$ or $3, 4$).
notes: Confuses the difference of the roots with $p$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $(\alpha - \beta)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2}$ for $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$.

en.q: If $T : \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is a linear transformation of $\mathbb{R}^4$ onto $\mathbb{R}^3$, then the nullity of $T$ is:
en.explanation: Onto means rank $T = \dim\mathbb{R}^3 = 3$. By rank–nullity, nullity $= \dim\mathbb{R}^4 - \text{rank} = 4 - 3 = 1$.
notes: A map from a larger space cannot be one-one.
facts: Rank–nullity: $\operatorname{rank}T + \operatorname{nullity}T = \dim(\text{domain})$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q25 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If the straight line $y = mx$ lies outside the circle $x^2 + y^2 - 20y + 90 = 0$, then the value of $m$ will satisfy:
en.explanation: Centre $(0, 10)$, radius $\sqrt{100 - 90} = \sqrt{10}$. The line $mx - y = 0$ is outside if its distance from the centre exceeds the radius: $\frac{10}{\sqrt{1 + m^2}} > \sqrt{10} \iff 1 + m^2 < 10 \iff |m| < 3$.
notes: Also allows large negative $m$, which cut the circle.
This is the condition for cutting the circle (reversed inequality).
facts: A line misses a circle when the perpendicular distance from the centre is greater than the radius.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q26 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: The solution of the differential equation $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 - 7\frac{dy}{dx} + 12 = 0$ is:
en.explanation: With $p = \frac{dy}{dx}$: $p^2 - 7p + 12 = (p - 3)(p - 4) = 0$, so $y = 3x + c$ or $y = 4x + c$. Together: $(y - 3x - c)(y - 4x - c) = 0$, and since $c$ is arbitrary we may write $-c$ as $c$: $(y - 4x + c)(y - 3x + c) = 0$.
notes: Sign error: the roots are $p = 3$ and $4$, not $-3$ and $-4$.
facts: An equation solvable for $p$ splits into first-degree factors $p - f_i(x, y) = 0$; the general solution is the product of their solutions with one constant.

en.q: The function $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 4$ is decreasing in the interval:
en.explanation: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)$, which is negative exactly when $1 < x < 3$. So $f$ decreases on $(1, 3)$.
notes: Sign error in the roots of $f'(x) = 0$.
facts: $f$ decreases where $f'(x) < 0$; for a quadratic $f'$ with positive leading coefficient, that is between its roots.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q28 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If $f(x) = ax + b$ and $f(f(f(x))) = 8x + 21$ and if $a, b$ are real numbers, then $a + b$ is equal to:
en.explanation: $f(f(x)) = a(ax + b) + b = a^2x + ab + b$, and $f(f(f(x))) = a^3x + a^2b + ab + b$. Comparing with $8x + 21$: $a^3 = 8 \Rightarrow a = 2$ (the only real root), and $(4 + 2 + 1)b = 21 \Rightarrow b = 3$. Hence $a + b = 5$.
facts: For $f(x) = ax + b$, the $n$-fold composite is $a^n x + b(a^{n-1} + \dots + a + 1)$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q29 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: A particle moves along the curve $x = t^3 - 2$, $y = t^2 + t$, $z = 2t + 1$. The component of its acceleration at $t = 1$ in the direction $\hat i - \hat j + \hat k$ is:
en.explanation: $\vec r = (t^3 - 2, t^2 + t, 2t + 1)$, $\vec v = (3t^2, 2t + 1, 2)$, $\vec a = (6t, 2, 0) = (6, 2, 0)$ at $t = 1$. Component along $\hat i - \hat j + \hat k$: $\frac{(6, 2, 0)\cdot(1, -1, 1)}{\sqrt3} = \frac{4}{\sqrt3}$.
notes: Forgets to divide by $|\hat i - \hat j + \hat k| = \sqrt3$.
facts: Component of $\vec a$ along $\vec b$ is $\frac{\vec a \cdot \vec b}{|\vec b|}$.

en.q: The volume of the solid generated by revolving the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ about the $x$-axis is:
en.explanation: $V = \pi\int_{-a}^a y^2dx = \pi\int_{-a}^a b^2\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{a^2}\right)dx = \pi b^2\left(2a - \frac{2a}{3}\right) = \frac43\pi ab^2$ (a prolate spheroid).
notes: Dimensionally an area times $\pi$, not a volume.
This is the volume about the $y$-axis (the minor axis).
path: 7.6 Volumes and surfaces of solids of revolution — formulas
facts: About the major axis: $\frac43\pi ab^2$; about the minor axis: $\frac43\pi a^2b$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q31 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: In $\triangle ABC$, $A = 30^\circ$, $B = 60^\circ$, then $a : b : c$ is:
en.explanation: $C = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 60^\circ = 90^\circ$. By the sine rule, $a : b : c = \sin A : \sin B : \sin C = \frac12 : \frac{\sqrt3}{2} : 1 = 1 : \sqrt3 : 2$.
notes: Interchanges $b$ and $c$: the largest side $c$ is opposite the largest angle $C = 90^\circ$.
Takes the sides proportional to the angles $30^\circ : 60^\circ : 90^\circ$ instead of their sines.
facts: Sine rule: $a : b : c = \sin A : \sin B : \sin C$ (the sides are proportional to the sines of the opposite angles, not to the angles).

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q32 · asked in UP PGT 2011

en.q: The point of intersection of the two lines given by $2x^2 - 5xy + 2y^2 - 3x + 3y + 1 = 0$ is:
en.explanation: The point is the centre: $\frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = 4x - 5y - 3 = 0$ and $\frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = -5x + 4y + 3 = 0$. Adding: $-x - y = 0$, so $y = -x$, and $9x = 3$: $\left(\frac13, -\frac13\right)$. Check by factors: $(2x - y - 1)(x - 2y - 1) = 0$, and both lines pass through $\left(\frac13, -\frac13\right)$.
notes: Sign slip in the $y$-coordinate (it does not satisfy $x - 2y - 1 = 0$).
facts: The two lines of a pair meet at the point where $\frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = 0$.

en.q: If the kinetic energy of a body is increased by 300%, its momentum increases by:
en.explanation: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$, so $p = \sqrt{2mK}$. An increase of 300% makes $K$ four times as large; then $p$ becomes $\sqrt4 = 2$ times as large, an increase of 100%.
notes: Takes momentum proportional to kinetic energy.
Would need the kinetic energy to become 9 times as large.
Would need the kinetic energy to become 2.25 times as large.
facts: $K = \frac{p^2}{2m}$: for a fixed mass, momentum varies as the square root of the kinetic energy.

en.q: The differential equation of all straight lines passing through the origin is:
en.explanation: The lines are $y = mx$, with one arbitrary constant $m$. Differentiating once: $\frac{dy}{dx} = m$. Eliminating $m$: $y = x\frac{dy}{dx}$.
notes: Its solutions are $y = Ce^x$, not lines.
Its solutions are the hyperbolas $xy = C$.
Its solutions are the hyperbolas $y^2 - x^2 = C$.
facts: A family with $n$ arbitrary constants gives a differential equation of order $n$: differentiate $n$ times and eliminate the constants.

en.q: The particular integral of $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 4y = \cos 2x$ is:
en.explanation: $\frac{1}{D^2 + 4}\cos2x$ fails ($D^2 = -4$), so use the case of failure: $\frac{x}{2D}\cos2x = \frac x2\int\cos2x\,dx = \frac x4\sin2x$. Check: for $y = \frac x4\sin2x$, $y'' = \cos2x - x\sin2x$ and $y'' + 4y = \cos2x$.
facts: $\frac{1}{D^2 + a^2}\cos ax = \frac{x}{2a}\sin ax$ and $\frac{1}{D^2 + a^2}\sin ax = -\frac{x}{2a}\cos ax$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q36 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: In the expansion of $\left(\frac{x^3}{4} - \frac{2}{x^2}\right)^9$, the 4th term from the end is:
en.explanation: There are 10 terms, so the 4th from the end is the $10 - 4 + 1 = 7$th from the beginning: $T_7 = {}^9C_6\left(\frac{x^3}{4}\right)^3\left(-\frac{2}{x^2}\right)^6 = 84 \cdot \frac{x^9}{64} \cdot \frac{64}{x^{12}} = \frac{84}{x^3}$.
facts: The $r$th term from the end of $(a + b)^n$ is the $(n - r + 2)$th term from the beginning.

en.q: The value of $\cos^2 48^\circ - \sin^2 12^\circ$ is:
en.explanation: $\cos^2A - \sin^2B = \cos(A + B)\cos(A - B)$. So $\cos^248^\circ - \sin^212^\circ = \cos60^\circ\cos36^\circ = \frac12 \cdot \frac{\sqrt5 + 1}{4} = \frac{\sqrt5 + 1}{8}$.
facts: $\cos^2A - \sin^2B = \cos(A + B)\cos(A - B)$; $\cos36^\circ = \frac{\sqrt5 + 1}{4}$, $\sin18^\circ = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$.

src.label: Expected PGT 2 · Q38 · asked in UP PGT 2021

en.q: If $B$ is a matrix such that $B^2 = B$ and $A = I - B$, then which of the following is not correct?
en.explanation: $A^2 = (I - B)^2 = I - 2B + B^2 = I - B = A$, so $A$ is idempotent and $A^2 = I$ is false (unless $B = O$). Also $AB = B - B^2 = O$ and $BA = B - B^2 = O$.
notes: Correct: this is the false statement.
True: $A^2 = I - 2B + B^2 = I - B = A$.
facts: If $B$ is idempotent, so is $I - B$, and $B(I - B) = (I - B)B = O$.

en.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform rectangular lamina of mass $M$ and sides $2a$ and $2b$, about the line through its centre parallel to the side $2a$, is:
en.explanation: Cut the lamina into thin strips parallel to the axis. A strip at distance $y$ from the axis ($-b \le y \le b$) has mass $\frac{M}{2b}\,dy$, so $I = \int_{-b}^{b}\frac{M}{2b}\,y^2\,dy = \frac{M}{2b}\cdot\frac{2b^3}{3} = \frac{Mb^2}{3}$ (like a rod of length $2b$ about its middle).
notes: Uses the half-side parallel to the axis; the distances from the axis run up to $b$.
This is about the axis through the centre perpendicular to the lamina.
This is about the side $2a$ itself: $\frac{Mb^2}{3} + Mb^2$ by parallel axes.
facts: Rectangle $2a \times 2b$, axes through the centre: $\frac{Mb^2}{3}$ (parallel to $2a$), $\frac{Ma^2}{3}$ (parallel to $2b$), $\frac{M(a^2 + b^2)}{3}$ (perpendicular to the plane).

en.q: Match List – I with List – II. List – I: a. $\sinh^{-1}\frac43$, b. $\cosh^{-1}\frac54$, c. $\tanh^{-1}\frac13$, d. $\coth^{-1}2$. List – II: I. $\frac12\log3$, II. $\frac12\log2$, III. $\log2$, IV. $\log3$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: a – III, b – IV, c – I, d – II
a – I, b – II, c – III, d – IV
a – IV, b – III, c – II, d – I
a – IV, b – II, c – III, d – I
en.explanation: $\sinh^{-1}x = \log(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1})$: $\sinh^{-1}\frac43 = \log\left(\frac43 + \frac53\right) = \log3$. $\cosh^{-1}x = \log(x + \sqrt{x^2 - 1})$: $\cosh^{-1}\frac54 = \log\left(\frac54 + \frac34\right) = \log2$. $\tanh^{-1}x = \frac12\log\frac{1 + x}{1 - x}$: $\tanh^{-1}\frac13 = \frac12\log2$. $\coth^{-1}x = \frac12\log\frac{x + 1}{x - 1}$: $\coth^{-1}2 = \frac12\log3$. So a – IV, b – III, c – II, d – I.
notes: Matches the lists in their printed order.
path: 10.10 Inverse circular and inverse hyperbolic functions

en.q: Forces of 5 N due east, 12 N due north and 10 N due west act on a particle. The magnitude of their resultant is:

Each power $x^k$ ($k \le 3$) of $e^x$ meets $x^{3-k}$ of the second factor, so the coefficient of $x^3$ is $1 + \frac1{1!} + \frac1{2!} + \frac1{3!} = 1 + 1 + \frac12 + \frac16 = \frac83$.

en.q: From a uniform circular disc of radius $a$, a circular hole of radius $\frac a2$ is cut out, the hole touching the rim of the disc. The centre of gravity of the remaining portion is at a distance from the centre of the disc equal to:
en.explanation: Masses are proportional to areas: the whole disc $\pi a^2$ at the centre $O$, the hole $\frac{\pi a^2}{4}$ with centre at distance $\frac a2$ from $O$. For the remainder, $\bar x = \frac{\pi a^2 \cdot 0 - \frac{\pi a^2}{4}\cdot\frac a2}{\pi a^2 - \frac{\pi a^2}{4}} = \frac{-a^3/8}{3a^2/4} = -\frac a6$: at distance $\frac a6$ from $O$, on the side away from the hole.
notes: Divides by the mass of the whole disc instead of the remaining mass.
Takes the masses proportional to the radii instead of the areas.
Places the centre of the hole on the rim (distance $a$) instead of at $\frac a2$.
facts: For a body with a part removed: $\bar x = \frac{m_1x_1 - m_2x_2}{m_1 - m_2}$ ($m_1$ the whole, $m_2$ the part removed).

en.q: The angle between the two lines whose direction cosines satisfy $2l + 2m - 3n = 0$ and $2lm - n^2 = 0$ is:
en.explanation: From the first, $n = \frac{2(l + m)}{3}$. Then $2lm = \frac{4(l + m)^2}{9}$, i.e. $4l^2 - 10lm + 4m^2 = 0$, so $(2l - m)(l - 2m) = 0$. If $m = 2l$: $n = 2l$, direction ratios $(1, 2, 2)$. If $l = 2m$: $n = 2m$, direction ratios $(2, 1, 2)$. Hence $\cos\theta = \frac{2 + 2 + 4}{3 \cdot 3} = \frac89$.
notes: That needs $\cos\theta = \frac12$; the direction ratios $(1, 2, 2)$ and $(2, 1, 2)$ give $\frac89$.
The direction ratios are not perpendicular: their dot product is 8.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: For lines given by a linear and a quadratic relation in $l, m, n$: eliminate one cosine, factor the quadratic in the other two, then use $\cos\theta = \frac{a_1a_2 + b_1b_2 + c_1c_2}{\sqrt{\sum a_1^2}\sqrt{\sum a_2^2}}$.

en.q: A smooth sphere of weight $W$ rests between two smooth planes inclined at angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ to the horizontal, the planes meeting in a horizontal line below the sphere. The reaction of the plane inclined at $\alpha$ is:
en.explanation: Each reaction is normal to its plane and passes through the centre, so $R_\alpha$ makes the angle $\alpha$ and $R_\beta$ the angle $\beta$ with the vertical, on opposite sides of it. The angles between the forces are $\alpha + \beta$ ($R_\alpha$, $R_\beta$), $180^\circ - \beta$ ($R_\beta$, $W$) and $180^\circ - \alpha$ ($R_\alpha$, $W$). Lami's theorem: $\frac{R_\alpha}{\sin(180^\circ - \beta)} = \frac{W}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$, so $R_\alpha = \frac{W\sin\beta}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$ (and $R_\beta = \frac{W\sin\alpha}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$).
notes: This is the reaction $R_\beta$ of the other plane.
Takes the reactions at the angles $\alpha$, $\beta$ to the horizontal instead of the vertical.
Drops the factor $\frac{1}{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}$: right only when $\alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$.
path: 15.2 Three forces in equilibrium: Lami's theorem
facts: Lami's theorem: three forces in equilibrium at a point satisfy $\frac{P}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{Q}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R}{\sin\gamma}$, each force over the sine of the angle between the other two; a smooth surface pushes along its normal.

en.q: If the area of the triangle with vertices $(k, 0)$, $(4, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$ is 4 square units, then the values of $k$ are:
en.explanation: Area $= \frac12\left|\begin{vmatrix} k & 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\right| = \frac12|8 - 2k|$. Setting it equal to 4: $|8 - 2k| = 8$, so $8 - 2k = \pm8$, giving $k = 0$ or $k = 8$.
notes: Uses only $8 - 2k = -8$; the determinant may have either sign.
Uses only $8 - 2k = 8$; the determinant may have either sign.
Sign error in expanding the determinant.
facts: Area of a triangle $= \frac12|\Delta|$, $\Delta$ the determinant of the vertex coordinates with a column of 1s; solve $\Delta = \pm 2 \times$ area.

en.q: $\int_0^{\pi/2} \sin^6 x\,dx$ is equal to:
en.explanation: For even $n$: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx = \frac{(n - 1)(n - 3)\cdots1}{n(n - 2)\cdots2}\cdot\frac\pi2$. For $n = 6$: $\frac{5 \cdot 3 \cdot 1}{6 \cdot 4 \cdot 2}\cdot\frac\pi2 = \frac{15}{48}\cdot\frac\pi2 = \frac{5\pi}{32}$.
notes: Drops the factor $\frac\pi2$, which belongs to even powers.
facts: $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^nx\,dx = \frac{n - 1}{n}\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{n-2}x\,dx$; the factor $\frac\pi2$ appears only for even $n$.

en.q: If $\int \frac{2^x}{\sqrt{1 - 4^x}}\,dx = k\sin^{-1}(2^x) + c$, then $k$ is equal to:
en.explanation: Put $2^x = t$, $2^x\log 2\,dx = dt$: $\int\frac{dt}{\log 2\sqrt{1 - t^2}} = \frac{1}{\log 2}\sin^{-1}t + c$. So $k = \frac{1}{\log 2}$.
facts: $\frac{d}{dx}a^x = a^x\log a$.

en.q: The line $3x + 4y = 7$ divides the line segment joining the points $(1, 2)$ and $(-1, 3)$ in the ratio:
en.explanation: Let $L(x, y) = 3x + 4y - 7$: $L(1, 2) = 4$, $L(-1, 3) = 2$. Equal signs mean both points are on the same side, so the division is external, in the ratio $4 : 2 = 2 : 1$. Check: dividing externally in $2 : 1$ gives $\left(\frac{2(-1) - 1}{1}, \frac{2 \cdot 3 - 2}{1}\right) = (-3, 4)$, and $3(-3) + 4 \cdot 4 = 7$.
notes: Both points are on the same side of the line, so the division is external.
Inverts the ratio: it is $L_1 : L_2 = 4 : 2$.
Both the ratio and the kind of division are wrong.
facts: The line $L = 0$ divides the join of $P_1$, $P_2$ in the ratio $-L(P_1) : L(P_2)$; a negative ratio means external division.

en.q: Which of the following statements are correct? a. If $A \subseteq B$, then $A \cup B = B$. b. If $n(A) = m$, then the power set of $A$ has $2^m$ elements. c. $A \times B = B \times A$ for all non-empty sets $A$ and $B$. d. $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
en.explanation: a: every element of $B$ is in $A \cup B$, and $A \subseteq B$ adds nothing new, so $A \cup B = B$ (true). b: each of the $m$ elements is either in a subset or not, giving $2^m$ subsets (true). c: ordered pairs change when the sets are swapped; with $A = \{1\}$, $B = \{2\}$ we get $\{(1,2)\} \ne \{(2,1)\}$ (false). d: the distributive law (true). So a, b and d only.
notes: Leaves out b and d, which are true, and keeps c, which is false.
c is false, so 'all four' cannot be right.
facts: $A \times B = B \times A$ only when $A = B$ (or one of them is empty); the Cartesian product is not commutative.

en.q: If $y = \cos(3\cos^{-1}x)$, then $\dfrac{d^3y}{dx^3}$ is equal to:
en.explanation: Put $\cos^{-1}x = \theta$: $y = \cos3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta = 4x^3 - 3x$. Then $y' = 12x^2 - 3$, $y'' = 24x$, $y''' = 24$.
notes: Treats $y$ as a quadratic; it is a cubic, so the third derivative is a non-zero constant.
facts: $\cos(3\cos^{-1}x) = 4x^3 - 3x$ (the Chebyshev polynomial $T_3$).

en.q: The system of equations $x + y + z = 6$, $x + 2y + 3z = 10$, $x + 2y + \lambda z = \mu$ has no solution if:
en.explanation:
Subtracting the second equation from the third: $(\lambda - 3)z = \mu - 10$. If $\lambda 
e 3$ there is a unique solution. If $\lambda = 3$ and $\mu = 10$, the third equation repeats the second (infinitely many solutions). If $\lambda = 3$ and $\mu 
e 10$, we get $0 = \mu - 10 
e 0$: no solution.
notes: $\lambda \ne 3$ already gives a unique solution, whatever $\mu$ is.
Then the third equation repeats the second: infinitely many solutions.
Then the coefficient determinant is non-zero: a unique solution.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: $|A| = 0$ is needed for no solution; then the system is inconsistent if $\operatorname{rank}[A|B] > \operatorname{rank}A$.

en.q: $\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{(1 + x)^{1/x} - e}{x}$ is equal to:
en.explanation: $\frac1x\log(1 + x) = 1 - \frac x2 + \frac{x^2}{3} - \dots$, so $(1 + x)^{1/x} = e \cdot e^{-x/2 + x^2/3 - \dots} = e\left(1 - \frac x2 + O(x^2)\right)$. Hence $\frac{(1 + x)^{1/x} - e}{x} \to -\frac e2$.
notes: Uses $(1 + x)^{1/x} \to e$ in the numerator too early.
Sign error in the expansion of $\log(1 + x)$.
facts: $(1 + x)^{1/x} = e\left(1 - \frac x2 + \frac{11x^2}{24} - \dots\right)$.

en.q: The equation of the ellipse whose foci are $(\pm 2, 0)$ and eccentricity is $\frac12$ is:
notes: Uses $b = ae = 2$ instead of $b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$.
Takes $a = 2$ (the focal distance) as the semi-major axis.
Puts the major axis along the $y$-axis; the foci are on the $x$-axis.
facts: Ellipse: foci $(\pm ae, 0)$ and $b^2 = a^2(1 - e^2)$.

en.q: Let $S, T : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be the linear maps $S(x, y) = (x + 2y,\ y)$ and $T(x, y) = (y,\ x)$. Then $(ST - TS)(x, y)$ is:
en.explanation: $ST(x, y) = S(T(x, y)) = S(y, x) = (y + 2x,\ x)$ and $TS(x, y) = T(x + 2y,\ y) = (y,\ x + 2y)$. Subtracting: $(ST - TS)(x, y) = (2x,\ -2y)$. (With matrices: $[S][T] - [T][S] = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$.)
notes: Composition of linear maps is not commutative in general.
facts: $(ST)(v) = S(T(v))$: apply $T$ first; the matrix of $ST$ is $[S][T]$, and in general $ST \ne TS$.

en.q: The area of the triangle with vertices $A(1, 1, 1)$, $B(1, 2, 3)$ and $C(2, 3, 1)$ is:
en.explanation: $\overrightarrow{AB} = (0, 1, 2)$, $\overrightarrow{AC} = (1, 2, 0)$, $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = (1 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 2,\ 2 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1) = (-4, 2, -1)$, of magnitude $\sqrt{21}$. Area $= \frac12\sqrt{21}$.
notes: This is the area of the parallelogram on $AB$ and $AC$.
facts: Area of triangle $ABC = \frac12|\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}|$.

en.q: The dimension of the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ spanned by the vectors $(1, 2, 1)$, $(2, 1, 0)$ and $(3, 0, -1)$ is:
en.explanation: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 1(-1) - 2(-2) + 1(-3) = 0$, so the three vectors are dependent; indeed $(3, 0, -1) = 2(2, 1, 0) - (1, 2, 1)$. The first two are not proportional, so they form a basis of the span: dimension 2.
notes: Only the zero space has dimension 0.
Two of the vectors, e.g. $(1, 2, 1)$ and $(2, 1, 0)$, are not parallel.
Assumes the three vectors are independent; $(3, 0, -1) = 2(2, 1, 0) - (1, 2, 1)$.
facts: Dimension of a span = rank of the matrix whose rows are the vectors.
